tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (ICLR 2021, per the CLBF paper's reference [38]; arXiv 2006.03176v2). Section 4.1 plots PLBF against a theoretically optimal Bloom filter (standard Bloom filter space divided by log2 e) and Appendix E.1 (Fig. 4) against standard Bloom filters. All the quoted multipliers vs sandwiched LBF and AdaBF appear verbatim in Section 4.1. The repo has only the parameter-optimization algorithm, not the experiment code, so this cannot be A.

corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed at ICLR 2021. The repo README says 'ICLR 2020', which is wrong; the CLBF paper cites it as ICLR 2021. The repo has only plbf_algo.py (threshold/FPR optimizer) and a README. It has no LICENSE file (reference/study only) and no experiment or benchmark code. The headline multipliers are against learned variants (sandwiched LBF, Ada-BF), not a raw Bloom filter. The 'optimal Bloom filter' curve is analytical (standard Bloom filter space / log2 e), and the standard-Bloom-filter comparison (Appendix E.1, Fig. 4) is shown only as a plot. The model is an sklearn random forest, sized by its pickle file. Last commit was in 2022-06, more than 3 years ago.

notes: Numbers check out exactly against arXiv Section 4.1. The only fixes are the venue year (ICLR 2021, not 2020) and maintenance status: the last commit on 2022-06-29 is more than 3 years before 2026-09-26, so the repo is abandoned, not stale. Metadata confirmed via gh: no license, 7 stars, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: These are first-party README numbers from the project's own go test benches (ribbon_bench_test.go BenchmarkPaper_*). The Bloom and Xor figures are textbook constants in a comparison table; no Bloom or Xor filter is benchmarked anywhere in the repo. Methodology is partial: Go version and flags are unpinned, and hardware is given only as 'Apple M3 Pro' and 'x86 Xeon Platinum' with no model. This is not peer-reviewed and not a third-party suite, so C rather than B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: w=128 at n=1e6 stores 7.334 bits/key (4.749% over the 7-bit minimum for r=7). It compares this with Bloom's 9.6 bits/key 'at the same FPR' and claims a 23.6% space saving. The 9.6 bits/key is the analytical Bloom value at 1% FPR, not a measured Bloom run, and r=7 actually gives FPR of about 0.78%, so the FPRs are not matched. Build is 106.3 ns/key (Apple M3 Pro). Query at n=1e6 is 43.2/31.7 ns/op positive/negative (x86 Xeon Platinum). At n=1e8, w=128 reaches 7.512 bits/key (7.314% overhead).
corrections.hardware: Build/Space tables on Apple M3 Pro (ARM64); Query table on an x86 Xeon Platinum host (exact CPU model not stated); absolute ns/op not comparable across the two tables
corrections.compiler_and_flags: go test -bench (go.mod declares go 1.24.2); the Go toolchain version and flags actually used for the published runs are not stated
corrections.caveats: This is a third-party Go reimplementation of the standard Ribbon filter (Dillinger & Walzer 2021, arXiv:2103.02515; it mirrors RocksDB ribbon_impl.h). It is distinct from BuRR (lorenzhs/BuRR, bumped ribbon retrieval), which is already catalogued, so it is not a duplicate. It is not a fork, and the repo was created 2026-03. The Bloom/Xor comparison is analytical only (a table of textbook bits/key constants); no baseline filter is benchmarked. Build and query figures come from two different hosts. The README's claim of 'at the same FPR' is loose because r=7 gives about 0.78% FPR, while 9.6 bits/key is Bloom's figure at 1%.

notes: It is a distinct implementation, not BuRR, and has its own measured numbers for itself only; the baseline side is theoretical. The default branch main was last committed 2026-07-17 (release v1.0.10 on 2026-07-18). The record's 2026-08-01 date comes from the non-default branch DhruvilK7-patch-1, so the repo is still active. MIT license and 15 stars confirmed.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The official code exists at github.com/atsukisato/CascadedLBF (first author's account; the README names the paper). It includes the classical Bloom filter baseline benchmark (experiment/bloom/construct_bloom.cpp, test_bloom.cpp, scripts/bloom/), and docker_run_all.sh reproduces all of the paper's results. Paper Section 6 states GCC 11.4.0, -O3, single-threaded, on an Intel Core i9-11900H @ 2.50 GHz. The quoted 17% figure is against PLBF; the classical Bloom filter appears only as a plotted Fig. 5 baseline.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4.0 with -O3, single-threaded (paper Section 6); repo builds with CMake Release inside an Ubuntu 22.04 Docker image
corrections.hardware: Linux, Intel Core i9-11900H @ 2.50 GHz, 64 GB RAM
corrections.claimed_speedup: At the same FPR, CLBF uses up to 17% less memory than the best PLBF configuration, for example on Ember at F=0.005. It cuts reject time by up to 14.6x vs PLBF under the default XGBoost setting, and by up to 65x across the appendix model variants. Construction takes 1.003x-1.23x longer than existing LBFs. A classical Bloom filter (fastfilter_cpp) is plotted as a baseline in Fig. 5, but no CLBF-vs-Bloom ratio is quoted. PLBF is described as the most memory-efficient LBF under a fixed model; G-PLBF matches CLBF on memory vs FPR.
corrections.workload: Memory-vs-FPR (target F from 0.1 to 0.001) and memory-vs-reject-time trade-offs on the URL, Ember and Higgs datasets (14 datasets in the appendix), using XGBoost models and 10,000 held-out test non-keys. Baselines are all in C++: classical Bloom filter (fastfilter_cpp), PLBF (via Fast PLBF), Sandwiched LBF, G-PLBF, Ensemble LBF, PHBF and HABF.
corrections.caveats: The record said there was no code, but that was wrong. The official implementation is https://github.com/atsukisato/CascadedLBF (Apache-2.0, C++, Docker-based reproduction scripts for CLBF and all baselines, 0 stars, created 2026-01). The repo_url should be set to it, but that field cannot be corrected here. The paper itself does not link the repo. The headline memory figure is against PLBF, not a classical Bloom filter. Reject time includes ML inference, so a plain Bloom filter may still reject faster. The source is arXiv v2 (2026-08-24), and no peer-review venue was confirmed.

notes: The key finding is that code exists: set repo_url to https://github.com/atsukisato/CascadedLBF (owner matches first author Atsuki Sato, who also owns FastPLBF) and rekey the id if the pipeline allows. The quoted 17% is confirmed verbatim (abstract, Section 6, Fig. 5 caption: Ember F=0.005). The record's 'strongest prior baseline' wording is softened because G-PLBF is comparable.
